summary: This document updates RFC 7001 by creating a registry for property types in the Authentication-Results email header field, rather than limiting use to the original small set. It was replaced by RFC 7601.

plainLanguage.summary: A list that only had a few fixed words now gets an official place to add new ones. This RFC does that for email checking results. It was later replaced.

questions: what are ptype values in authentication-results
subtitle: Creating a registry for types of information in email authentication results.

tldr.problem: The Authentication-Results email header field in RFC 7001 had only a fixed set of property types, limiting future extensions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7410 creates an IANA registry where new property types ('ptypes') can be registered and documented, allowing the header to carry new kinds of authentication information.
tldr.outcome: Email authentication systems can now report new types of authentication properties. Systems that do not understand a property type simply ignore it. This RFC was replaced by RFC 7601.

today: RFC 7410 is a Proposed Standard. It has been replaced by RFC 7601.

sections.title: Authentication Results and Property Types
sections.content:
RFC 7001 defines the Authentication-Results header field, which presents the results of authentication mechanisms in a machine-readable format. It separates the output of authentication processes from later filtering or sorting systems.

The original specification enumerated a small fixed set of property types (ptypes): body, header, policy, and smtp. These indicated what part of the message or SMTP transaction was being authenticated. RFC 7410 allows new ptypes to be added through an IANA registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Email checking systems use a special header to report what they checked and whether it passed. It had only four choices; now there is a place to add more.

sections.title: The Registry and New Property Types
sections.content:
The IANA 'Email Authentication Property Types' registry is subject to Expert Review. Each entry requires the ptype token to be registered, a description of the information it covers, and optionally a reference to the defining document.

The initial ptypes are body (property from message body), header (property from message header), policy (local policy mechanism), and smtp (property from SMTP command). When a system encounters a ptype it does not understand, it ignores the result reported with that ptype.
sections.plainLanguage: New words can be added to the list through expert review. Old systems just ignore words they do not know.

sections.title: Security of Unknown Types
sections.content:
Systems that encounter unknown ptype tokens may either prevent message delivery or ignore the unknown portions and continue processing. The choice depends on whether the system considers unknown ptypes a threat.

The advice is generally to ignore unknown ptypes, since ignoring unknown information is safer than rejecting messages based on information that cannot be understood.
sections.plainLanguage: Old email systems that see a new word have two choices: throw away the message or ignore the new word. Ignoring is safer.
